Master Feature Engineering Field Guide

The Master Architecture Guide to Feature Engineering in Machine Learning

From Rolling Windows & Cyclical Time Waves to Domain Interaction Ratios and Leakage-Free Scaling Pipelines.

1. Rolling Windows: Denoising, Volatility, Envelopes & Memory

A rolling feature extracts moving statistical signals over a lookback window $W$. To guarantee zero data leakage, rolling features must strictly shift by 1 step (shift(1)) so the current row's target is never visible during window aggregation.

A. Rolling Mean (Denoising)

Filters out high-frequency noise and isolates macro trends.

Mean = (1 / K) * ∑ x_(t-i)

B. Rolling StdDev (Volatility)

Detects market regime shifts, stability, and risk jumps.

Std = √[ (1 / (K-1)) * ∑ (x - µ)² ]

C. Rolling Min/Max (Dynamic Corridor)

Establishes resistance ceilings and support floors to trigger breakout alerts.

D. Rolling Sum (Cumulative Saturation)

Tracks system memory (e.g. soil moisture, fraud spend limits, API quotas).

2. Cyclical Time Features: Encoding Time as a Continuous Circle

Calendar metrics like Day of Year (1 to 365) or Hour of Day (0 to 23) are naturally cyclical. Naive numeric representations create an artificial 364-unit gap between Dec 31st and Jan 1st. We project these variables onto a unit circle using Sine and Cosine components.

sin_time = sin(2 * π * time / Period)
cos_time = cos(2 * π * time / Period)
Why Year is Excluded from Sine/Cosine:

Months and hours repeat in loops ($12 ightarrow 1$). Year is linear and monotonic ($2023 ightarrow 2024$). Year measures long-term secular drift (e.g., climate change), whereas Sine/Cosine measures annual seasonality.

3. Domain Interaction Features: Creating Physical Feature Columns

Machine learning models perform significantly better when we combine raw variables into high-level physical formulas rather than forcing decision trees to rediscover physics from scratch.

Engineered Feature Column Formula Physical Signal to ML Model
Diurnal Temp Range (DTR) temp_max - temp_min Clear-sky radiational cooling vs overcast cloud cover
Apparent Heat Gap apparent_temp - raw_temp Human heat index & wind-chill humidity distortion
Water Balance Ratio precipitation / (evapotranspiration + 1e-5) Net soil hydration & drought saturation index

4. Mathematical Transformations: Fixing Skewed Distributions

Variables like rainfall, snowfall, or financial transaction amounts are heavily right-skewed with extreme zero-inflation. Linear models and neural networks fail on these. We apply log or power transformations to compress extreme spikes into bell-shaped Gaussian curves.

Log Transform (log1p)

y = ln(1 + x): Compresses exponential Spikes while preserving 0s safely.

Yeo-Johnson Power Transform

Optimizes power parameter $\lambda$ to normalize distributions, supporting negative numbers (e.g. sub-zero temperatures).

5. Categorical Encoding Taxonomy

Translating non-numeric text labels into model-digestible numerical matrices.

Encoding Technique Mechanism Best Used For Leakage Guardrail
One-Hot Encoding Creates binary 0/1 indicator columns per category Low cardinality (< 10 categories: Season, Day) None (Independent of Target)
Ordinal Encoding Assigns ordered integers (1, 2, 3) Categories with natural rank (Light, Severe, Extreme) None (Independent of Target)
Frequency Encoding Replaces category with its occurrence count High cardinality (Zip codes, User IDs) None (Independent of Target)
Target Encoding Replaces category with mean of Target ($y$) Complex high-dimensional tabular data MUST use K-Fold Out-of-Fold on Train set only!

6. Master Production Feature Engineering Pipeline (Polars & Pandas)

A complete, leak-free feature engineering pipeline implementing Lags, Rolling Windows, Cyclical Waves, and Physical Interactions.

import polars as pl
import numpy as np

def build_master_feature_pipeline(df: pl.DataFrame) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """
    Production-grade, leak-free feature pipeline in Polars.
    Guarantees strict temporal boundaries (shift(1)) and zero future leakage.
    """
    return (
        df.sort("time")
        .with_columns([
            # 1. TARGET
            pl.col("temperature_2m_max (°C)").alias("target_today_max_temp"),

            # 2. LAG FEATURES (Strictly shift 1+)
            pl.col("temperature_2m_max (°C)").shift(1).alias("temp_lag1"),
            pl.col("temperature_2m_max (°C)").shift(2).alias("temp_lag2"),

            # 3. ROLLING FEATURES (Shifted first!)
            pl.col("temperature_2m_max (°C)").shift(1).rolling_mean(7).alias("temp_roll_mean_7"),
            pl.col("temperature_2m_max (°C)").shift(1).rolling_std(14).alias("temp_roll_std_14"),
            pl.col("temperature_2m_max (°C)").shift(1).rolling_max(30).alias("temp_roll_max_30"),

            # 4. CYCLICAL TIME FEATURES (Sine & Cosine)
            (2 * np.pi * pl.col("time").dt.ordinal_day() / 365.0).sin().alias("sin_day_of_year"),
            (2 * np.pi * pl.col("time").dt.ordinal_day() / 365.0).cos().alias("cos_day_of_year"),

            # 5. DOMAIN PHYSICAL INTERACTIONS
            (pl.col("temperature_2m_max (°C)") - pl.col("temperature_2m_min (°C)")).alias("dtr_range"),
            (pl.col("apparent_temperature_max (°C)") - pl.col("temperature_2m_max (°C)")).alias("heat_index_gap"),

            # 6. SKEWNESS CORRECTION (Log transform)
            (pl.col("precipitation_sum (mm)") + 1.0).log().alias("log_precipitation")
        ])
        .drop_nulls()
    )
